title: Why faults snap
teaches: How a stuck fault stores the plates' motion as bent rock and releases it in an earthquake, what sets an earthquake's size, and why soft ground shakes harder

blocks.text: At 5:12 in the morning on 18 April 1906, the ground under San Francisco shook for about a minute. Gas mains broke, and the fires that followed burned for three days and destroyed most of the city. Out in the countryside the earthquake left a stranger kind of damage. North of the city, in the valleys of Marin County, a crack ran across the fields in a nearly straight line, and everything that crossed it had been cut and shifted sideways. A fence near Olema was broken in two, with one half moved 2.6 metres along the crack from the other. Roads, rows of trees and a dam had been offset in the same way, by up to about 6 metres, always in the same direction: the land west of the crack had moved north.

Geologists traced the crack for more than 400 kilometres, from San Juan Bautista south of San Francisco to Shelter Cove on the north coast. It followed a line of long straight valleys, sag ponds and offset streams that Andrew Lawson of the University of California had already noticed and, in 1895, named after one of them, the San Andreas Valley. The 1906 earthquake had broken along a **fault**, a fracture in the crust along which the rocks on either side move past each other.

blocks.caption: The San Francisco Bay region and the north coast of California. The red line is the stretch of the San Andreas Fault that broke in 1906, dashed where it runs under the sea.

options.title: The 1906 break
options.alt: A shaded relief map of the coast of northern California from Monterey Bay to Cape Mendocino. A red line runs northwest from San Juan Bautista, past San Francisco just offshore, through Tomales Bay and up the coast to Point Arena, then out to sea to Shelter Cove.

blocks.text: The surveyors of the US Coast and Geodetic Survey had something more. Across the Bay Area they had laid out a network of survey marks on hilltops, measured in the 1850s and 1860s and again in the 1870s and 1880s, using **triangulation**[^triangulation] to fix each mark's position to within a few centimetres. After the earthquake they measured the network once more. The marks had moved in the earthquake, as everyone expected. What nobody expected was that they had also moved between the two older surveys, decades before the earthquake, with no earthquake to move them.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: The 1906 San Francisco earthquake broke the San Andreas Fault along more than 400 km, shifting the land west of it north by up to about 6 m.
A fault is a fracture in the crust along which the rocks on either side move past each other.
Survey marks near the fault had moved between surveys in the decades before the earthquake, without any earthquake.

blocks.text: Harry Fielding Reid, a geophysicist at Johns Hopkins University, took on the survey records for the state commission that investigated the earthquake. In 1910 he published his explanation. The movements between the old surveys had been smooth and slow: marks far from the fault had moved most, marks near it least, and none had moved where the fault itself would later break. Then, in the earthquake, the pattern reversed: marks close to the fault jumped the furthest, and marks far away barely moved.

Reid saw that the two patterns fitted together. Far from the fault, the land on each side was moving steadily, the west side north and the east side south. The fault itself was stuck, held shut by friction and by the weight of the rock pressing its two sides together. So the rock near the fault could not slide; it bent instead, like a ruler held at both ends and pushed sideways in the middle. Year by year the bent rock stored more energy as elastic **strain**, the deformation of a solid that springs back when the force is removed. A fence built straight across the fault in 1850 would by 1906 have been bent into a long, gentle S, too gentle for anyone to notice. When the strain became greater than the fault's friction could resist, the fault slipped, and in seconds the rock on each side sprang back to an unbent shape in its new position. Reid called this **elastic rebound**. The earthquake was not the cause of the movement; it was the moment when the fault caught up with movement that had been going on for a century.

blocks.caption: A fence built across a locked fault, seen from above, as the plates move past each other at 3 cm a year. The movements are greatly exaggerated: the zone that bends is tens of kilometres wide, and the bend is a few metres.
blocks.task: Play the years until the fault slips

blocks.text: Plate tectonics later explained the steady motion that Reid could only measure. The San Andreas is a transform fault (lesson 11) on the boundary between the Pacific plate and the North American plate, which move past each other at about 5 centimetres a year; the San Andreas carries more than half of that, and other faults nearby carry the rest. Today a network of GPS receivers measures the bending Reid inferred from a few survey marks. Stations far from the fault move steadily with their plates, while stations near it barely move. The change from one to the other is spread across a band some tens of kilometres wide, just as Reid's bent ruler predicts. That band is wide because only the top 15 kilometres or so of the fault is cold and brittle enough to stick. Below that the rock is hot enough to flow, and creeps steadily past.

Reid also suggested how to forecast the next earthquake: build a line of piers across the fault, watch them bend, and expect the fault to slip again when the bend matches what 1906 released. Seismologists tried a version of this, and it turned out to be harder than it sounds.[^parkfield] Faults do not break at exactly the same strain each time, and an earthquake on one fault changes the strain on its neighbours. Geologists can say how fast strain is building on a fault, and roughly how often it has broken in the past. They cannot yet say which year it will break next.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Elastic rebound: the plates move steadily, but the fault is stuck, so the rock beside it bends and stores strain.
When the strain overcomes the fault's friction, the fault slips in seconds and the rock springs back: an earthquake.
GPS shows the bending today: a band tens of kilometres wide across the fault, because only the top 15 km or so of the fault is brittle enough to lock.
How fast strain builds can be measured; exactly when a fault will break cannot yet be predicted.

blocks.text: A heavy box dragged across a floor with an elastic rope does the same thing. You pull steadily, and the box stays put while the rope stretches; then the box lurches forward, stops, and the rope starts stretching again. Engineers call this **stick-slip**. A fault behaves like the box: the plates are the steady pull, the bending rock is the rope, and each lurch is an earthquake.

blocks.caption: A block pulled through a spring across a rough floor, standing for a fault loaded by plates moving 3 cm a year. The graph below shows how far the fault has slipped (red) against how far the plates have moved (blue).
blocks.task: Run at least 300 years with a fault that holds 2 m or less, and again with one that holds 5 m or more

blocks.text: How strongly a fault sticks decides how its earthquakes come. Over the long run every fault must keep up with its plates: if the plates move 3 metres in a century, the fault must slip 3 metres in that century, in whatever steps. So a fault that sticks weakly slips often and a little at a time, and a fault that sticks hard stores more strain and releases it in rare, large earthquakes. Some stretches of fault barely stick at all. Between San Juan Bautista and Parkfield, the San Andreas **creeps**: it slides about 3 centimetres a year without large earthquakes, slowly tearing apart fences, roads and buildings that stand across it.

The size of an earthquake depends on how much fault slips and how far. Seismologists measure it as **moment magnitude**,[^magnitude] which is calculated from the area of the fault that broke, how far it slipped, and the stiffness of the rock. Each step of one on the scale means about 32 times more energy. A magnitude 5 earthquake breaks a patch of fault a few kilometres across and slips it a few centimetres. The 1906 earthquake, about magnitude 7.9, broke more than 400 kilometres of fault to a depth of about 12 kilometres and slipped it several metres. The largest earthquakes on Earth, magnitude 9 and above, need even more fault, and only the gently sloping faults of subduction zones, which lesson 19 takes up, are big enough.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Faults load and release like a box dragged by an elastic rope: stick-slip.
A fault that sticks harder has larger, rarer earthquakes; over the long run every fault keeps up with its plates.
Some fault segments creep steadily without large earthquakes.
Magnitude grows with the area of fault that breaks and how far it slips; each whole step is about 32 times more energy.

blocks.text: On the morning of 19 September 1985, a magnitude 8.0 earthquake broke the subduction zone off the Pacific coast of Mexico, in the state of Michoacán. The towns nearest the fault were damaged, but the worst destruction was 350 kilometres away, in Mexico City. Hundreds of buildings collapsed there, and at least 5,000 people died; some estimates are several times higher. Yet across much of the city the shaking was mild. Whole districts on its western hills came through almost untouched, while blocks in the centre were flattened.

The difference was in the ground. Mexico City stands in a high basin that once held a lake, Lake Texcoco, which the Aztecs built their capital on and the Spanish drained. The old lake bed is a layer of very soft, waterlogged clay tens of metres thick. Earthquake waves arriving from the hard rock below slow down when they enter the soft clay, and as they slow they grow taller, just as ocean waves grow taller as they reach shallow water. The clay layer also has a rhythm of its own. Like a bowl of jelly, it sways back and forth at its own natural **period** (the time one full sway takes), about two seconds in the worst-hit part of the city, and the long, steady waves from the distant earthquake set it ringing. Instruments on the lake bed recorded shaking about five times stronger than on the rock of the hills a few kilometres away.

blocks.caption: The same earthquake waves arriving under buildings on bedrock, stiff soil, and soft lake clay. Each ground rings at its own period; a building sways at a period of about 0.1 second per storey. The shadows show how far each building sways.
blocks.task: Find the building height that sways hardest on the lake clay

blocks.text: Buildings sway at a natural period of their own as well; a rule of thumb used by engineers is roughly a tenth of a second for each storey. A building whose period is close to the ground's is pushed again at the top of each sway, and its motion builds up: **resonance**, the same effect that lets small, well-timed pushes swing a child high. In 1985 most of the buildings that fell were between about 6 and 15 storeys tall. Their periods were already close to the clay's, and they grew longer as the buildings cracked, until building and ground swayed together. Low houses and tall towers nearby survived the same ground.

The same lesson has been learned in other cities. In the 1989 Loma Prieta earthquake south of San Francisco, the Marina District, built on sand and rubble dumped into the bay, shook far harder than the rocky hills around it. Maps of where the ground is soft are now part of every city's earthquake planning, and building codes ask for stronger buildings there.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Soft ground, such as old lake clay or fill, amplifies earthquake waves: they slow down and grow larger as they enter it.
A layer of soft ground rings at its own natural period; Mexico City's lake clay rings at about 2 seconds.
Buildings sway at about 0.1 s per storey; when a building's period matches the ground's, resonance makes it sway hardest.

blocks.caption: Six questions on faults and shaking
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Between the surveys of the 1850s–60s and the 1870s–80s, survey marks far from the San Andreas Fault moved, while marks next to it hardly moved. What did Reid conclude?
choices: The fault was stuck while the plates moved, so the rock beside it was bending and storing strain
The survey of the 1860s had been badly made
Small earthquakes too weak to feel had moved the far marks
items.why: If the land far away moves steadily and the fault does not slip, the rock between must bend. The 1906 earthquake released that bend.

items.ask: A fence crossed the fault in a straight line before 1906. Just before the earthquake, what shape was it in?
choices: Bent gently into an S across a wide zone, but unbroken
Straight and unbroken, exactly as built
Already broken and offset at the fault
items.why: The rock bent with the plates for decades while the fault stayed stuck, and the fence bent with the rock. It only broke when the fault slipped.

items.ask: Two faults move at the same long-term rate. One creeps and the other sticks hard. How do their earthquakes differ?
choices: The one that sticks hard has rarer, larger earthquakes; the creeping one has few or none that are large
They have the same earthquakes, because they move at the same rate
The creeping one has larger earthquakes, because it moves all the time
items.why: Both must keep up with the plates. A fault that holds more strain before slipping releases it less often but in bigger slips.

items.ask: What makes one earthquake larger in magnitude than another?
choices: A larger area of fault breaking and slipping further
A deeper starting point, whatever the size of the break
items.why: Moment magnitude is calculated from the area of fault that broke, how far it slipped, and the stiffness of the rock. Distance from a city changes the damage, not the magnitude.

items.ask: In 1985 Mexico City was 350 km from the earthquake. Why was the damage there so severe?
choices: The city stands on soft old lake clay, which amplified the shaking and rang in time with many buildings
The fault ran directly under the city centre
Mexico City is closer to the fault than the coastal towns
items.why: On the lake bed the waves slowed, grew larger and set the clay swaying at about 2 seconds, close to the sway of mid-height buildings. The rocky hills of the same city shook far less.

items.ask: On the same soft lake clay, which building is most at risk from resonance: a 2-storey house, a 12-storey office block, or a 50-storey tower?
items.why: At about 0.1 s per storey, a 12-storey building sways at about 1.2 seconds, and cracking lengthens it towards the clay's 2 seconds. The house is far too stiff to match, and the tower far too slow.

summary: **Faults store motion as bent rock.** The plates move steadily, the fault stays stuck, and the rock beside it bends.
**An earthquake is the snap back.** When strain beats friction, the fault slips in seconds and the rock springs back: Reid's elastic rebound.
**GPS sees the bending.** Stations far from a locked fault move with their plates; near it they barely move.
**Stick-slip sets the rhythm.** Faults that stick hard have rarer, larger earthquakes; some faults creep instead.
**Size comes from area and slip.** Each step of magnitude is about 32 times more energy.
**Soft ground amplifies shaking.** Waves slow down and grow in soft clay or fill.
**Ground and buildings can resonate.** A building that sways at the ground's period, at about 0.1 s per storey, shakes hardest.

triangulation.title: Triangulation
triangulation.text: Surveyors fixed the positions of hilltop marks by measuring the angles between them with a telescope on a precise circle (a theodolite). If one distance in a network of triangles is known exactly, the angles give all the others. Before satellite positioning this was how countries were mapped, and repeating the angles years later showed which marks had moved.

parkfield.title: The Parkfield experiment
parkfield.text: The small town of Parkfield, on the San Andreas in central California, had magnitude 6 earthquakes in 1857, 1881, 1901, 1922, 1934 and 1966, roughly every 22 years. In 1985 the US Geological Survey predicted the next one for about 1988, give or take five years, and surrounded the fault with instruments to catch it. It came in 2004, sixteen years late, and gave no clear warning beforehand. The instruments still produced the most detailed record of a fault breaking that had ever been made.

magnitude.title: From Richter to moment magnitude
magnitude.text: Charles Richter's 1935 scale was based on how far the needle of a particular seismograph swung at a set distance from the earthquake. It stops growing for very large earthquakes, because the waves it measures stop growing too. Moment magnitude, introduced in 1979 by Thomas Hanks and Hiroo Kanamori, is calculated from the seismic moment: the rock's rigidity times the area that slipped times the average slip. It was set up to agree with Richter's scale for moderate earthquakes.
